konular: Prefill vs. decode and KV cache

sorular.soru: A very deep post-norm model is hard to train. Which change helps with this most directly?
secenekler: Replace LayerNorm with RMSNorm, but keep the norm after the residual add
Move the norm before each sublayer, so x passes straight to the output
Replace the ReLU FFN with SwiGLU, so each token gets a learned gate
Replace absolute positions with RoPE, so attention sees token distance
sorular.aciklama: Pre-norm keeps a direct residual path, so x and its gradients can skip every norm on their way through the deep stack. Using RMSNorm after the add still leaves a norm on the main path, so the flow problem stays.

sorular.soru: Modern LLMs put RMSNorm before attention and before the FFN. What is its main job there?
secenekler: It adds position information, so the next layer knows where each token is
It decides which feature channels can pass and which ones are blocked
It shrinks the stored keys and values, so the KV cache uses less memory
It keeps the scale of each token vector steady for the next layer
sorular.aciklama: RMSNorm divides each vector by its root mean square and skips the mean step of LayerNorm, so each sublayer gets inputs of a steady scale. Deciding which channels pass is the job of the SwiGLU gate, not of the norm.

sorular.soru: The old ReLU FFN and the modern SwiGLU FFN work in different ways. What do they have in common?
secenekler: Both update each token on its own, without looking at other tokens
Both use a learned gate that decides how much of each feature passes
Both set every negative value to zero before the final projection
Both mix information across tokens, like a second attention step
sorular.aciklama: Both FFNs transform each token separately, and only attention moves information between tokens. The learned gate is the part SwiGLU adds, and the ReLU FFN does not have one.

sorular.soru: The words 'red car' appear at the start of one text and near the end of another. Why can RoPE give the two words a similar attention score in both texts?
secenekler: RoPE rotates only the value vectors, so the scores do not see position
RoPE adds a position vector once at the input, and deeper layers forget it
RoPE makes the score depend on the gap between the words, not their slots
RoPE removes position from the score, so only the word meaning counts
sorular.aciklama: RoPE rotates the query and the key by their positions, so their dot product depends on the content and on the offset between them. Position still matters, but as the distance between the words, not as their slot number.

sorular.soru: GQA and MQA let several query heads share the same key and value heads. What is the main reason for this?
secenekler: The KV cache gets smaller, so each new token needs less memory to read
Each query head sees fewer tokens, so attention needs less calculation
Shared heads act like experts, so only a few of them run for each token
Shared heads are rebuilt at each step, so no KV cache is needed
sorular.aciklama: Fewer key and value heads mean fewer K/V entries to store and to read at every decoding step. Each query head still looks at all the tokens, so the saving does not come from seeing fewer tokens.

sorular.soru: Among MHA, GQA and MQA, MQA has the smallest KV cache. Why might a team still pick GQA?
secenekler: GQA keeps more query heads than MQA, so it can read the text in more ways
GQA keeps a few K/V heads, so query heads do not all read the same K/V
GQA packs K/V into a learned latent, so its cache is even smaller
GQA gives each query head its own K/V head, so nothing is shared
sorular.aciklama: In MQA every query head reads one shared K/V head, which limits variety, while GQA shares within groups and still keeps the cache small. MQA also keeps many query heads, so the number of query heads is not the difference.

sorular.soru: An MoE model stores many expert FFNs, but each token needs only a little GPU work. Why?
secenekler: All experts run for each token, but each one is too small to cost much
The experts share one set of weights, so only one expert is really stored
The router lets tokens skip attention, so each token only runs an FFN
A router picks a few experts for each token, so most of them do not run
sorular.aciklama: The router scores the experts, runs only the top few for each token and mixes their outputs. Running every expert would make the GPU work grow with each new expert, which is what MoE avoids.

sorular.konu: Prefill vs. decode and KV cache
sorular.soru: Why can the model read the whole prompt in one pass, but must write its answer one token per pass?
secenekler: The prompt goes into the KV cache, but answer tokens can never be cached
The prompt goes to the large model, but a small draft model writes the answer
The prompt tokens are all known, but each new token needs the one before
The prompt is usually short, but the answer is almost always much longer
sorular.aciklama: In prefill all prompt tokens are already there, so they pass through the model together. In decode the next token does not exist until the step before it ends, and its K/V is cached as well.

sorular.konu: Prefill vs. decode and KV cache
sorular.soru: A model without a KV cache writes a long answer. Each new token takes longer than the one before. Why?
secenekler: Each step runs the whole text again, and that text grows at every step
Each step updates the weights again, as if the model were still training
Each step reads all the weights again, and the weights grow with the text
Each step rotates vectors by larger angles, and big angles cost more work
sorular.aciklama: Without a cache, the K/V of every earlier token is calculated again at each step, so the work grows with the answer. The weights keep the same size and are not updated during inference.

sorular.konu: Prefill vs. decode and KV cache
sorular.soru: In a long chat, the user sends a short follow-up: 'Can you shorten that?' How can prefix caching make the reply start sooner?
secenekler: It reuses the earlier reply as it is, so the model does not run again
It drops the earlier turns, so the model reads only the short new message
It reuses the K/V of the earlier turns, so only the new tail is processed
It splits the earlier turns into chunks, so other users can run in between
sorular.aciklama: The K/V of the earlier turns is already stored, so prefill only has to handle the new tail. The old turns are not dropped, because the new tokens still attend to their cached K/V.

sorular.soru: FlashAttention gives the same result as standard attention. Where does its speed-up come from?
secenekler: It skips token pairs with low scores, so it does less math than usual
It stores the attention scores with fewer bits, so they take less space
It reuses the scores from earlier steps, so they are not calculated again
It works on small tiles on the chip, so less data goes to slow GPU memory
sorular.aciklama: Standard attention writes a big score table to slow GPU memory and reads it back. FlashAttention keeps small tiles on the chip and updates the softmax as it goes, so the math is the same and no token pair is skipped.

sorular.soru: With PagedAttention, the KV blocks of one request can sit anywhere in GPU memory. How does the system still find them in the right order?
secenekler: The GPU moves the blocks back into one row before every decode step
A block table records which physical page holds each logical block
A prefix cache keeps a second copy of the blocks in their first order
RoPE marks each block with its position, so attention sorts them again
sorular.aciklama: Each request has a block table, so its logical blocks can live in physical pages anywhere in memory and a new block can take any free page. Moving the blocks back into one row would bring back the copying and waste that paging avoids.

sorular.soru: A server runs the same group of requests until the longest one ends, so slots of finished requests sit empty. Which technique fixes this waste?
secenekler: Continuous batching, which lets new requests take the freed slots
Chunked prefill, which splits long prompts into parts between decodes
Prefix caching, which reuses the K/V of a start that requests share
PagedAttention, which gives KV blocks to requests only as they grow
sorular.aciklama: Continuous batching lets the scheduler choose active requests at every step, so a waiting request takes a slot as soon as one frees up. PagedAttention fixes wasted KV memory, not empty batch slots.

sorular.soru: A server makes many tokens per second in total, but one user still waits a long time for the first token. How is this possible?
secenekler: Throughput counts only decode, while TTFT counts only the gaps between tokens
Throughput is the gap between tokens, while TTFT is the time of the full answer
Throughput grows with prompt length, while TTFT does not depend on the prompt
Throughput adds up all users, while TTFT is the start delay of one request
sorular.aciklama: Throughput is the total tokens or finished requests per second for the whole server, so it can stay high while one request waits in a queue or a long prefill. The gaps between tokens are ITL, not TTFT.

sorular.soru: A new user sends a very long prompt. While the model reads it, other users see long pauses between their tokens. What does chunked prefill change?
secenekler: It cuts the long prompt into parts and keeps only the most useful ones
It reads the long prompt in parts, and other users decode in between
It saves the long prompt's K/V, so later turns can reuse it quickly
It gives the long prompt to a small draft model that reads it faster
sorular.aciklama: Chunked prefill runs the long prompt block by block and fits other users' decode steps in between, so their token gaps (ITL) stay short. No part of the prompt is dropped, since every block still goes through prefill.

sorular.soru: A student wants to run a big model on a laptop with little memory. Which technique helps most directly?
secenekler: Speculative decoding, which drafts tokens with a small model
Continuous batching, which fills free slots with new requests
Quantization, which stores each weight with fewer bits
PagedAttention, which gives out KV blocks only when needed
sorular.aciklama: Fewer bits per weight make the model much smaller in memory, but each weight becomes a little less exact. PagedAttention only cuts wasted KV-cache space, so the weights stay just as large.

sorular.soru: In speculative decoding, why is it cheaper for the large model to check the draft tokens than to write them itself?
secenekler: It checks all draft tokens in one pass, but writing needs a pass per token
It checks only the first draft token, and it trusts the rest without checks
It checks the drafts with fewer bits, so each check reads less memory
It lets the small model check the drafts, so its own weights are not read
sorular.aciklama: Writing goes one token per pass, but the draft tokens are already known, so the target can score them all in one pass. It still checks every draft token and fixes the first one it rejects.

sorular.soru: A university chatbot gets prompts from many students at the same time. Why does a tool like vLLM fit better than a local tool like Ollama?
secenekler: vLLM is a newer, larger LLM, so it gives better answers than local models
vLLM serves each request alone, one after another, so answers do not mix
vLLM batches many requests and manages KV memory for all of them at once
vLLM gives similar questions one shared answer, so it saves GPU work
sorular.aciklama: vLLM is a serving engine that schedules many requests with continuous batching and paged KV memory. It is not a new or larger model, so the answers come from the same LLM.
